'''Francis Louis Halzen''' (born 23 March 1944) is a Belgian-American physicist who has worked in both theoretical and experimental [[particle physics]], including [[high-energy astrophysics]].  Born in Belgium, he was educated at the [[Catholic University of Leuven (1834–1968)|Catholic University of Leuven]] and worked as a scientific associate at [[CERN]] before moving to the United States, where he has been a professor at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] since 1972.  Since 2001 he has been the principal investigator and co-spokesperson of the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory]], the world's largest [[neutrino]] detector, based at the [[Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station]] in [[Antarctica]].  He received the 2026 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/halzen/facts/ |access-date=6 October 2026 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261006150059/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/halzen/facts/ |archive-date=6 October 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Halzen-Neutel (cropped).jpg|thumb|Halzen with a replica of Galileo's telescope, 2025]]
Francis Louis Halzen<ref>{{cite web | last=Kölbel | first=David Beck und Ralf | title=Nobelpreis für Physik: Auszeichnung für Nachweis von "Geistern aus dem All" | publisher=tagesschau.de | date=6 October 2026 | url=https://www.tagesschau.de/wissen/physiknobelpreis-francis-halzen-100.html | language=de | access-date=7 October 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Belgian Physicist Wins Nobel Prize In Physics For Cosmic Particle Discovery | website=FinanzNachrichten.de | date=6 October 2026 | url=https://www.finanznachrichten.de/nachrichten-2026-10/69767784-belgian-physicist-wins-nobel-prize-in-physics-for-cosmic-particle-discovery-020.htm | language=de | access-date=7 October 2026| quote=Copyright(c) 2026 RTTNews.com}}</ref> was born on 23 March 1944 in [[Tienen]], Belgium.<ref name=":1"/>  He graduated from the [[Catholic University of Leuven (1834–1968)|Catholic University of Leuven]] with an [[MSc]] Physics degree in 1966, a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1969.  His doctoral dissertation, written in [[Dutch language|Dutch]], was titled ''Gebroken symmetrieën van hadronen – dynamica van het π N kanaal'' ("Broken symmetries of [[Hadron|hadrons]]: Dynamics of the π N channel").<ref>[https://lib.is/lbsn996766760101471/representation?libis=11:1:1& "Gebroken symmetrieën van hadronen -dynamica van het PII Pl-nucleon kanaal". Halzen, Francis (author); KUL. Faculteit wetenschappen. (other)
s. n. Leuven: s.n. 1968. [Library catalogue entry, University of Leuven]. </ref>  Between 1969 and 1971, he worked as a scientific associate at [[CERN]].  In 1972, Halzen completed his ''agrégation de l'enseignement supérieur'', which at the time was the [[habilitation]] required to advance to senior research and teaching positions in a Belgian university.<ref name="cv">{{cite web  | title= Francis Halzen: Curriculum Vitae | website=Academy of Europe | url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Halzen_Francis/CV | access-date=7 October 2026}}</ref>  

== Career ==
In 1972, Halzen was appointed as an assistant professor at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] (UW), in the United States.  He became a full professor at UW in 1977.  Since 1984 he has been director of UW's Institute for Elementary Particle Physics Research.  In 1987 he was promoted to the [[Gregory Breit]] Distinguished Chair.  Halzen's early research was focused on theoretical particle physics and [[nuclear physics]].{{Cn|date=October 2026}}  With British theoretical physicist [[Alan Martin (physicist)|Alan Martin]], Halzen co-authored ''Quarks and Leptons: An Introductory Course in Modern Particle Physics'' (1984), which soon became a standard textbook in particle physics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/alan-martin-11891/|title=Alan Martin|work=Fellows Directory|publisher=Royal Society|accessdate=4 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128114221/https://royalsociety.org/people/alan-martin-11891/|archive-date=28 November 2019|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Halzen |first=Francis |url=https://www.google.co.cr/books/edition/Quarks_and_Leptons/G7RvQgAACAAJ?hl=en |title=Quarks and Leptons: An Introductory Course in Modern Particle Physics |last2=Martin |first2=Alan Douglas |date=1984 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-81187-9 |language=en}}</ref>

Halzen also became a leading researcher in [[cosmic ray]] physics and [[astroparticle physics]].  He has published many papers on cosmic ray anomalies and [[quark matter]], on relations between particle physics and cosmic rays, on particles from [[Supernova|supernovae]], and on [[muon]] production in atmospheric [[Gamma ray|gamma-ray]] showers.<ref name="BalzanPrize2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.balzan.org/en/prizewinners/francis-halzen|title=2015 Balzan Prize for Astroparticle Physics including neutrino and gamma-ray observation|date=October 2015|accessdate=11 November 2018|work=[[Balzan Prize|International Balzan Prize Foundation]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190810195205/https://www.balzan.org/en/prizewinners/francis-halzen|archive-date=10 August 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>   

Halzen was appointed Vilas Research Professor in 2021. {{as of| October 2026}} he retains this position, as well as continuing in the roles of director of the Institute for Elementary Particle Physics Research and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor.<ref name=cv202610>{{cite web | title=Curriculum Vitae: Francis Halzen | url=https://user-web.icecube.wisc.edu/~halzen/CV/FH_longCV_05152026.pdf | access-date=7 October 2026| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261006222303/https://user-web.icecube.wisc.edu/~halzen/CV/FH_longCV_05152026.pdf| archive-date= 6 October 2026| url-status=live}}</ref>{{Independent source inline|date=October 2026}}

=== AMANDA ===
{{main|Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array}}
Halzen first learned about attempts by Russian scientists to detect neutrinos in [[Antarctica]], using radio antennas at their Antarctic research station to search for electric sparks resulting from cosmic [[Neutrino|neutrinos]] colliding with the ice.<ref name="NeutrinoHunters">{{cite book|last=Jayawardhana|first=Ray|author-link=Ray Jayawardhana|date=10 December 2013|title=Neutrino Hunters: The Thrilling Chase for a Ghostly Particle to Unlock the Secrets of the Universe|url=https://archive.org/details/neutrinohunterst0000jaya|url-access=registration|publisher=[[Scientific American]]|isbn=978-0-374-22063-1}}</ref> After determining these interactions would be too weak to register, in 1987 he started working on the AMANDA project, which proposed burying an array of light sensors deep in the Antarctic ice which is clear, dark, stable, sterile and free of background light.  That design was based on an idea by Soviet physicist [[Moisey Markov]], originally proposed in 1960 but never implemented, to look for high-energy neutrinos by putting [[Cherenkov detector|Cherenkov detectors]] into [[Lake Baikal]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Как нобелевского лауреата по физике 2026 года вдохновила идея советского ученого почти 70-летней давности. История открытия нейтрино |publisher=Meduza |date=6 October 2026 |url=https://meduza.io/feature/2026/10/07/kak-nobelevskogo-laureata-po-fizike-2026-goda-vdohnovila-ideya-sovetskogo-uchenogo-pochti-70-letney-davnosti |language=ru |access-date=11 October 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=IceCube and the Discovery of High-Energy Cosmic Neutrinos |first=Francis |last=Halzen |url=https://www.balzan.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/ABL8-Halzen-Download.pdf |access-date=11 October 2026 |page=34}}</ref>

This pilot AMANDA experiment was able to detect high-energy cosmic muons and neutrinos, but its measurements were affected by interference from [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]], as well as by air bubbles in the ice. These factors convinced Halzen that a much larger and deeper array would be needed, and in 2005 the AMANDA project became part of its successor project, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/advanced-physicsprize2026.pdf|title=Scientific background to the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 (pdf)|via=NobelPrize.Org|access-date=6 October 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261006123354/https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/advanced-physicsprize2026.pdf|archive-date=6 October 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== IceCube Neutrino Observatory ===
{{Main|IceCube Neutrino Observatory}}
[[File:IceCube Neutrino Observatory in 2023 02.jpg|thumb|IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole]]

In 2005, his team began construction of the IceCube project, designed to be 100 times larger than AMANDA, with a total volume of {{cvt|1|km3}} and buried up to {{convert|2400|m|ft}} deep. After six years of construction, IceCube became fully operational in 2011.<ref name="ox">{{cite web|url=https://www.physics.ox.ac.uk/news/icecube-celebrating-decade-discovery|title=IceCube: celebrating a decade of discovery|date=13 May 2021|access-date=6 October 2026|via=University of Oxford Department of Physics}}</ref> The most important result from IceCube was the clear breakthrough observation of high-energy neutrinos (about 100 times more energetic than the particles accelerated today at the world's most powerful machine, the LHC at CERN) in 2013, from as-yet-unidentified sources outside the galaxy. This discovery has stimulated the planning and development of even larger neutrino telescopes, both at the South Pole and deep underwater.<ref name="BalzanPrize2015" />

=== Other roles ===
Halzen has served on various advisory committees, including those for the [[Sudbury Neutrino Observatory|SNO]], Telescope Array and Auger-upgrade experiments, the [[Max Planck Society|Max Planck Institutes]] in Heidelberg and Munich, the [[Institute for Cosmic Ray Research|ICRR]] at the [[University of Tokyo]] in 1983 and 1987, the US Particle Physics Prioritization Panel and the ApPEC particle astrophysics advisory panel in Europe.<ref name="BalzanBio2015">{{cite web|url=https://www.balzan.org/en/prizewinners/francis-halzen/bio-bibliography-halzen|title=Francis Halzen: Biographical and Bibliographical Information|date=October 2015|accessdate=19 February 2020|work=[[Balzan Prize|International Balzan Prize Foundation]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180919124240/http://www.balzan.org/en/prizewinners/francis-halzen/bio-bibliography-halzen|archive-date=19 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Honours and awards ==
In 1994, Halzen became fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship?q=Francis%20Halzen&af=true|title=APS Fellows archive|work=[[American Physical Society]]|access-date=6 October 2026}}</ref> and elected to [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 April 2024 |title=National Academy of Sciences Elects Members and International Members |url=https://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2024-nas-election.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240430193331/https://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2024-nas-election.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=30 April 2024 |access-date=12 May 2024 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> in 2024. He has received many awards, including:
* 2013: ''Breakthrough of the Year Award'' by the journal ''[[Physics World]]'' for the first-time discovery of cosmic neutrinos beyond the [[Milky Way]]<ref name="PhysicsWorld2013">{{cite web|url=https://physicsworld.com/a/cosmic-neutrinos-named-physics-world-2013-breakthrough-of-the-year/|title=Cosmic neutrinos named Physics World 2013 Breakthrough of the Year|date=13 December 2013|accessdate=11 November 2018|work=[[Physics World]]|author=Hamish Johnston|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128114251/https://physicsworld.com/a/cosmic-neutrinos-named-physics-world-2013-breakthrough-of-the-year/|archive-date=28 November 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2015: [[Balzan Prize]]<ref name="BalzanPrize2015" />
* 2015: [[Cocconi Prize|Giuseppe and Vanna Cocconi Prize]] of the [[European Physical Society]] "for his visionary and leading role in the detection of very high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos, opening a new observational window on the Universe."<ref name="EPS2015">{{cite web|url=https://www.eps.org/blogpost/751263/213602/The-2015-EPS-HEPP-Prizes-are-announced|title=The 2015 EPS HEPP Prizes are announced|date=14 April 2015|accessdate=11 November 2018|work=[[European Physical Society]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128114228/https://www.eps.org/blogpost/751263/213602/The-2015-EPS-HEPP-Prizes-are-announced|archive-date=28 November 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2018: [[Bruno Pontecorvo Prize]] for significant contribution to the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory|IceCube]] detector construction and experimental discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos.<ref name="dlnp.jinr.ru">{{Cite web|url=https://dlnp.jinr.ru/en/175-slajdshou-na-glavnoj/647-bruno-pontecorvo-prize-2018-awards-to-professor-francis-halzen-university-of-wisconsin-madison-usa|title=Bruno Pontecorvo Prize 2018 awarded to Professor Francis Halzen (University of Wisconsin, Madison, USA)|website=dlnp.jinr.ru|access-date=10 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231104172552/https://dlnp.jinr.ru/en/175-slajdshou-na-glavnoj/647-bruno-pontecorvo-prize-2018-awards-to-professor-francis-halzen-university-of-wisconsin-madison-usa|archive-date=4 November 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2019: [[Yodh Prize]] of [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics|IUPAP]] for "his leadership and landmark contributions cleared a path for the emergence of neutrino astronomy."<ref>{{cite web|author=O'Keefe, Madeleine|title=Francis Halzen awarded the 2019 Yodh Prize|website=IceCube Neutrino Observatory|date=2 August 2019|url=https://icecube.wisc.edu/news/awards/2019/08/francis-halzen-awarded-2019-yodh-prize/}}</ref>
* 2021: [[Homi Bhabha Medal and Prize]] of [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics|IUPAP]] and [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research|TIFR]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://iupap.org/who-we-are/internal-organization/commissions/c4-astroparticle-physics/c4-awards/ |title=Homi Bhabha Medal and Prize, C4: Awards – IUPAP: The International Union of Pure and Applied Physics |date=17 February 2021 |access-date=7 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260921144320/https://iupap.org/who-we-are/internal-organization/commissions/c4-astroparticle-physics/c4-awards/ |archive-date=21 September 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* 2026: [[APS Medal for Exceptional Achievement in Research]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 December 2025 |title=Francis Halzen and the search for ghost particles |url=https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2025/12/medal-francis-halzen |access-date=9 December 2025 |website=www.aps.org}}</ref>
* 2026: [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin"<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Breeden |first=Aurelien |date=6 October 2026 |title=Nobel Prize in Physics Is Awarded to Francis Halzen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/science/nobel-prize-physics.html |access-date=6 October 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTi0PU_yPvU |title=Announcement of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics |date=14 September 2026 |last=Nobel Prize |access-date=6 October 2026 |via=YouTube |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261007060728/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTi0PU_yPvU |archive-date=7 October 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>
In 2005, the U.S. [[Advisory Committee on Antarctic Names]] named the [[Halzen Mesa]] (within the Insel Range in [[Victoria Land]], Antarctica) after Francis Halzen.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Antarctica Detail |url=https://geonames.usgs.gov/apex/f?p=gnispq:5:::NO::P5_ANTAR_ID:18739 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602220947/https://geonames.usgs.gov/apex/f?p=gnispq:5:::NO::P5_ANTAR_ID:18739 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |access-date=9 October 2026 |website=geonames.usgs.gov |language=en-us}}</ref>

=== Nobel Prize in Physics ===
In 2026, Halzen was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."<ref name=":1" />  In announcing the award, the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] credited Halzen's scientific leadership in developing IceCube as an instrument for neutrino astronomy. It explained that high-energy neutrinos can point us to distant astrophysical [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerators]], because neutrinos travel over cosmic distances without changing direction or losing energy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 – Press release |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/press-release/ |website=NobelPrize.org |date=6 October 2026 |access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref>
